title: Chapter 17 — That In Times Marked By Equality Of Conditions And Sceptical Opinions, It Is Important To Remove To A Distance The Objects Of Human Actions
paragraphs: Sceptical Opinions, It Is Important To Remove To A Distance The Objects Of Human Actions

In ages of faith the final end of life is placed beyond life itself. People of those ages therefore naturally, and almost involuntarily, grow accustomed to fixing their gaze for a long course of years on some unmovable object toward which they are constantly tending; and they learn by imperceptible degrees to suppress a multitude of small passing desires in order to be better able to satisfy that great and lasting desire which possesses them. When these same men turn to the affairs of this world, the same habits can be traced in their conduct. They tend to set up some general and definite aim for their actions here below, toward which all their efforts are directed; they do not turn from day to day to chase some new object of desire, but have settled designs they never tire of pursuing. This explains why religious nations have so often achieved such lasting results: while they were thinking only of the other world, they had discovered the great secret of success in this one. Religions give men a general habit of conducting themselves with an eye to the future; in that respect they are no less useful to happiness in this life than to felicity in the next — and this is one of their chief political characteristics.

But as the light of faith grows dim, the range of man's sight narrows, as though the end and aim of human actions were drawing daily closer within his reach. Once men have let themselves stop thinking about what is to come after life, they readily lapse into that complete and brutal indifference to the future which is only too conformable to certain tendencies of mankind. As soon as they have lost the habit of placing their chief hopes on remote events, they naturally seek to gratify their smallest desires without delay; and no sooner do they despair of living forever than they are disposed to act as if they were to exist only for a single day. In sceptical ages it is therefore always to be feared that men may give themselves up perpetually to their daily passing desires, and, wholly renouncing whatever cannot be acquired without sustained effort, may establish nothing great, permanent, and calm.

If the social condition of a people, under these circumstances, becomes democratic, the danger I have pointed out is thereby increased. When everyone is constantly striving to change his position — when an immense field for competition is thrown open to all — when wealth is amassed or dissipated in the shortest possible span of time amid the turmoil of democracy, visions of sudden and easy fortunes, of great possessions quickly won and lost, of chance in all its forms, haunt the mind. The instability of society itself fosters the natural instability of man's desires. Amid these perpetual fluctuations of his lot, the present grows on his mind until it hides the future from his sight, and his looks go no further than tomorrow.

In those countries where, unhappily, irreligion and democracy coexist, the most important duty of philosophers and of those in power is to strive constantly to set the objects of human action far beyond man's immediate reach. Constrained by the character of his country and his age, the moralist must learn to vindicate his principles from within that position. He must constantly endeavor to show his contemporaries that, even amid the perpetual commotion around them, it is easier than they think to conceive and execute sustained undertakings. He must teach them that although the look of mankind may have changed, the methods by which men may provide for their prosperity in this world are still the same; and that among democratic nations, as elsewhere, only by resisting a thousand petty selfish passions of the hour can the general and unquenchable passion for happiness be satisfied.

The task of those in power is no less clearly marked out. At all times it matters that those who govern nations act with a view to the future; but this is even more necessary in democratic and sceptical ages than in any others. By acting this way, the leading men of democracies not only make public affairs prosperous, but they also teach private individuals, by their example, the art of managing private concerns. Above all they must strive as much as possible to banish chance from the sphere of politics. The sudden and undeserved promotion of a courtier makes only a fleeting impression in an aristocratic country, because the aggregate institutions and opinions of the nation habitually compel men to advance slowly along tracks they cannot step off. But nothing is more pernicious than similar instances of favor displayed before a democratic people; they give a final impulse to the public mind in a direction in which everything already drives it. In times of scepticism and equality especially, the favor of the people or of the prince, which chance may bestow or chance withhold, ought never to stand in place of attainments or services. It is desirable that every advancement there should appear to be the result of some effort, so that no greatness may be too easily acquired, and that ambition should be obliged to fix its gaze long upon an object before it is satisfied. Governments must apply themselves to restoring to men that love of the future which religion and the state of society no longer inspire in them; and, without saying so, they must practically teach the community day by day that wealth, fame, and power are the rewards of labor — that great success stands at the furthest reach of long desires, and that nothing lasting is obtained except by toil. When men have grown accustomed to foresee from afar what is likely to happen in the world, and to feed on hopes, they can hardly confine their minds within the precise circumference of life, and are ready to break the boundary and cast their looks beyond it. I have no doubt that by training the members of a community to think of their future condition in this world, they would gradually and unconsciously be brought nearer to religious convictions. So the means that allow men, up to a certain point, to go without religion, are perhaps after all the only means we still possess for bringing mankind back, by a long and roundabout path, to a state of faith.
